lead: An FM signal carries its message in frequency, yet every practical detector works on amplitude. The trick is to convert the frequency deviation into an amplitude change and then envelope-detect it, as Unit 2 taught. One detuned tuned circuit does this — the slope detector. Two of them, balanced, do it better. The Foster-Seeley discriminator does it with a transformer whose secondary phase rotates with frequency, and the ratio detector adds one large capacitor for free limiting. Every FM broadcast receiver and every 10.7 MHz IF strip ends with one of these circuits.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for instantaneous frequency, Chapter 3.2 for deviation and bandwidth, and Unit 2 for the IF stage and the envelope detector.

sections.h3: Slope detector: one detuned tuned circuit

blocks.text: An FM detector is two blocks: a frequency-to-amplitude converter, then the diode envelope detector from Unit 2. The converter is a resonant circuit. Its voltage against frequency peaks at the resonant frequency f_r and falls away on both flanks, and near f_r each flank is almost a straight line.
Place the carrier f_c on a flank by tuning f_r a little to one side of f_c. As the FM signal swings around f_c, the output swings with it. Frequency deviation has become amplitude.

blocks.where: v_o is the detector output in volts; S is the slope sensitivity in volts per hertz (often written mV/kHz); f is the instantaneous frequency in Hz; f_r is the resonant frequency of the tuned circuit in Hz.

blocks.text: Two faults. The straight part is short, about the tuned-circuit bandwidth B = f_r/Q wide, so the circuit suits narrowband FM and distorts wideband broadcast FM with ±75 kHz deviation. And it is single-ended: AM on the incoming carrier, from noise or fading, comes straight out as audio. That is why an FM IF strip always ends in a limiter.
Raising Q steepens the slope, giving more volts per kHz, but shortens the straight part. That trade never goes away.

The balanced slope detector uses two tuned circuits, one resonant above f_c and one below, each with its own diode, and subtracts the outputs. The frequency terms have opposite signs, so the difference is steeper and straighter; the AM terms are equal and cancel. Output is zero at f_c. The cost is alignment: two primaries must be trimmed against each other.

One transformer, a tuned primary, and a secondary that is both tuned to f_c and centre-tapped. Let e_p be the primary voltage and e_s the secondary voltage. The centre tap splits e_s into two halves of e_s/2, in antiphase with each other.

A tuned secondary driven through mutual inductance does not hold its voltage in phase with e_p. At f_c, e_s is 90° out of phase with e_p. Above f_c the angle grows past 90°; below f_c it falls short. The secondary phase rotates with frequency, and that rotation is the mechanism.

Diode D1 sees the vector sum e_p + e_s/2; diode D2 sees e_p − e_s/2. Each diode with its RC load is an envelope detector, so the load voltages are the magnitudes V1 = |e_p + e_s/2| and V2 = |e_p − e_s/2|. The audio output is their difference, v_o = V1 − V2.

At f_c the two vectors have equal length and v_o = 0. Above f_c one grows while the other shrinks, so v_o > 0; below f_c the reverse, v_o < 0. Plotted against frequency this is an S-curve, odd about f_c, so the polarity of the output tells you which side of f_c the signal lies on. Hence the name frequency discriminator.

Linearity beats the slope detector. Near resonance the secondary phase varies almost linearly with frequency, and near 90° the difference of the two magnitudes varies almost linearly with the phase angle. Two linear laws multiplied give a linear detector over a wide band.

Amplitude: both V1 and V2 scale with input amplitude, so at f_c an amplitude change cancels in the subtraction. Away from f_c a residual AM term survives, so a limiter still precedes the circuit. Feeding the output through an integrator recovers the phase message, which is how the same circuit demodulates PM.

sections.h3: Ratio detector, and how the family compares

blocks.text: Reverse one diode and merge the two loads into a single resistor with a large capacitor C across all of it. Both diodes now conduct the same way round the loop, so the voltages add: C charges to V1 + V2, not V1 − V2.

The time constant R_L C is long compared with one audio cycle. V1 + V2 is therefore held almost constant. A sudden rise in input amplitude tries to raise both V1 and V2, but C absorbs it; only a slow drift is followed. The output, tapped from part of the load, then depends only on the ratio V1/V2, which depends only on frequency. That is the name, and that is the limiting: AM is squeezed out inside the detector, without a separate limiter stage.

The price: the load carries the sum, so audio output is roughly half that of a Foster-Seeley for the same input; the S-curve is slightly asymmetric; and the two diodes must be matched, because an imbalance charges C wrongly and shifts the operating point. For NBFM the Foster-Seeley is the usual choice, since narrow deviation already gives a small output.

figure.caption: The limited IF signal is split by the tuned transformer so that one diode sees the sum of the two voltages and the other the difference. Their difference is zero when the carrier sits exactly at the centre frequency and swings positive or negative with deviation.

spec.title: Foster-Seeley discriminator
spec.aria: The limited IF signal is split by a tuned transformer into two voltages that add on one diode and subtract on the other; their difference is the audio, and it is zero when the input sits exactly at the centre frequency.

examples.question: A slope detector uses a tuned circuit detuned so that the 10.7 MHz carrier sits on the straight part of the resonance curve, where the slope sensitivity is 25 mV per kHz. The FM signal deviates by ±75 kHz. Find the peak audio output voltage.
steps: The detector converts frequency deviation to voltage, so the output is slope × deviation.
Peak output V_p = S × Δf = 25 mV/kHz × 75 kHz = 1875 mV.
Convert to volts: 1875 mV ÷ 1000 = 1.875 V, about 1.9 V.
The output swings positive for positive deviation and negative for negative deviation, so the audio is a 1.875 V peak wave at the message frequency.
examples.answer: The peak audio output is 1875 mV, that is 1.875 V, about 1.9 V.
examples.check:
S = 25.0
df = 75.0
vp_mV = S * df
print(vp_mV)
print(vp_mV / 1000)
print(round(vp_mV / 1000, 1))

traps: A slope detector output is not zero at the carrier: it sits at a bias point on the flank. Only the balanced slope, Foster-Seeley and ratio detectors cross zero at f_c.
Units: 25 mV/kHz × 75 kHz = 1875 mV, not 1875 V. Divide by 1000 at the end.
The S-curve is linear only over a limited range. Beyond it the output flattens and then folds back, so a larger deviation does not give a larger output.
The Foster-Seeley secondary is tuned to the same f_c as the primary, not offset. The 90° phase shift comes from resonance, not from detuning.
The ratio detector gives about half the output and only modest limiting. Do not claim it removes all AM, or that it needs no limiter in a demanding receiver.

quiz.q: What does the limiter in front of an FM detector do, and why is it needed?
quiz.a: It strips amplitude variations caused by noise and fading and delivers a constant-amplitude signal, so the detector responds only to frequency. Without it a slope detector would output AM as audio.

quiz.q: Why is the Foster-Seeley circuit called a phase discriminator?
quiz.a: Its diodes compare the phase of the secondary voltage with the primary voltage, and that phase changes with frequency, so the output measures frequency offset.

quiz.q: Why must the carrier of a slope detector sit on the straight part of the resonance curve?
quiz.a: Output equals slope times deviation. Only where the curve is straight is the slope constant, so only there is the output proportional to deviation; on the curved part the audio is distorted.

quiz.q: How does a balanced slope detector reduce AM at its output?
quiz.a: Two tuned circuits sit on opposite flanks of f_c, each with a diode, and their outputs are subtracted. An amplitude change raises both outputs equally and cancels. A frequency change raises one and lowers the other, so the frequency effects add.

quiz.q: A Foster-Seeley discriminator gives +2.4 V at +40 kHz deviation and is linear in that range. What deviation gives −1.2 V?
quiz.a: Output ratio = −1.2 V ÷ 2.4 V = −0.5. Deviation = −0.5 × 40 kHz = −20 kHz.

quiz.q: A slope detector has sensitivity 15 mV/kHz and the deviation is ±25 kHz. Find the peak output in volts.
quiz.a: V_p = 15 mV/kHz × 25 kHz = 375 mV = 0.375 V peak.

quiz.q: Explain why the ratio detector gives roughly half the output of a Foster-Seeley, and what it gains in return.
quiz.a: The two diodes drive one load in series, so the load carries V1 + V2 and the output is tapped from part of it, halving the audio. The gain is that the large capacitor holds V1 + V2 constant, so the output follows only the ratio and AM is limited inside the detector without a separate limiter stage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern receivers sample the IF and do the same job in arithmetic: take the arctangent of the I and Q samples, then the difference of successive phase samples. This polar discriminator is the sum-and-difference phase comparison of the Foster-Seeley done in numbers, and it is what software-defined radio uses. Broadcast and two-way FM chips still keep a ratio or quadrature detector on the same die because it is cheap. Search for quadrature FM demodulator, polar discriminator, and ratio detector limiting to see the family tree.
